articleTitle: Optimisation of the synchronous reluctance motor geometry
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A machine is required which ideally utilises an induction motor stator, to take advantages of low manufacturing costs, and a synchronous rotor design, but with no windings, brushes or slip-rings, to maintain high reliability. A synchronous reluctance motor (synchrel motor) meets the mechanical requirements. One possible advantage of the synchrel motor is that for operation at or near zero speed, the external fan may not be needed. The authors describe research work involved in determining an optimum design for a synchrel motor for use in a high performance drive system which may compete with DC and vector control drives.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electronic load/excitation controller for a self-excited squirrel cage generator micro-hydro scheme
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A generating system has been described, which allows a 3 phase squirrel cage generator to be driven by a water turbine which also drives mechanical grain milling machines. The system guarantees a minimum of 386 W from one voltage regulated phase, over a speed range of 1350-1660 RPM a nominal regulated voltage of 210 V. The voltage is regulated by phase controlled dump loads on the other two phases, the heat from which can be used for cooking etc. Although there are limitations to the system such as regulator noise, unbalanced use of the generator, the system is simple, rugged, needs minimum maintenance and is cheap. Two such system have been operating satisfactorily in Nepal for two years. It is hoped that it will assist in increasing the quality of life of some of those in developing countries.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real time expert system for identifying rotor faults and mechanical influences in induction motor phase current
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors describe the background to the development of a knowledge-based system for distinguishing rotor faults and load influences in the stator current spectra of an induction motor. Data and case histories from up to 100 users of this rotor fault detection technique have been accumulated over the past three to four years. From a study of this invaluable collection of knowledge, new information, both fundamental and empirical, has been deduced to improve and enhance the existing diagnostic technique. This was possible by organising the knowledge using rule based techniques and making the information available in the form of expert system software for use in real-time with data gathering equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On-line detection of airgap eccentricity in 3-phase induction motors, by Park's Vector approach
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors introduce the use of the Park's Vector approach for detecting, online, airgap eccentricity in three-phase induction motors. In particular, experimental results, obtained by using a special fault producing test rig, show how the presence of static eccentricity can be diagnosed reliably by monitoring the current Park's Vector representation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Torque ripple minimisation methods in sinusoidal fed synchronous permanent magnet machines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In this paper, the authors present a torque ripple analysis method, based on an analytical solution of the equation which governs the magnetic field distribution in the different parts of the machine. The considered model corresponds in fact to a smooth pole and slotless stator structure. Nevertheless, if the stator is slotted, the model remains a usable approximate representation, in as much as the reluctance effects introduced by the slots are not considered. The proposed analysis is finally experimentally validated thanks to a modulatable model which permits the testing of different magnet arrangements and different winding structures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Motoring performance of the toroidal permanent-magnet machine 'Torus'
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Toroidal-stator permanent-magnet machines have been studied for a variety of applications which can benefit from their particularly short axial length and relatively high power-to-weight ratio. Both generator and motor duties have been studied. Several versions have been under study for some time at UMIST and have become referred to as Torus machines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A universal method for modelling electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors describe a universal method for composing a simulation model for any type of electrical rotating machine. Models for asynchronous machines, permanent magnet or excited synchronous machines, brushless and brush DC, stepping and variable reluctance motors are presented. A simulation model is needed when detailed interactions between driver circuitry, machine, load and controller are to be studied. In such cases it is usually not possible to transform the system into a solvable matrix differential equation. A general applicable transient machine model, interacting easily with existing models of its surroundings, the inverter and the mechanical load, is to be preferred.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The performance analysis of the single-phase, AC commutator-motor
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors look at the prediction of single-phase AC commutator motor performance. The technique adopted is that of a set of mutually coupled windings. The differential equations defining the current in the machine are solved numerically by Runge Kutta techniques. All the data required for the prediction of the performance is calculated from basic machine dimensions or is obtained from simple measurements performed on sample brushes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Iron losses in cage induction motors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors present experimental iron loss measurements and discuss the prediction of these in relation to the standard information provided by the steel manufacturers. The emphasis of the work is to develop semi-empirical methods of predicting the iron losses that are reliable and accurate to reasonably well-defined tolerances. These methods are based upon straight-forward experimental loss measurements and are particularly suitable for motor manufacturers where a routine program of testing steel lamination material can be carried out. Statistical variations in the iron losses for nominally identical lamination materials can thus be monitored and allowed for in the motor designs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A non-intrusive system (SMS) to monitor sparking along the brush/commutator interface of a DC machine
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: DC machines are widely used in industrial purposes due to their precise variable speed control characteristics and large overload capabilities. Quantitative assessment of commutation in DC machine, measured over the complete duty cycle has not been possible. Imperfect commutation usually causes sparking under or at the edge of the brushes. Such sparking can cause damage that is costly in material, labour and downtime. The authors describe the philosophy, principles of operation, hardware and synchronisation of data. They also describe the optical system used to monitor the speed of the machine. These generated signals from the speed monitoring circuit are used to mark the captured data, reference signal for frequency multiplication and speed monitoring are also going to be described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Assessment of induction motor cage fatigue life
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The induction motor is widely recognized as being inherently the most reliable motor for industrial drives. Attention to the detailed design of the rotor cage winding is necessary to realise the full potential for high reliability. Transient and steady state conditions must be considered with regard to the combined thermal and rotational stresses and their affect on the cage life. The author describes those mechanisms which lead to cage failure due to fatigue. The author describes how the stress levels may be calculated and how this in turn can be used to assess the fatigue life of a given design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of canned rotors in high speed permanent magnet machines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The design of high speed permanent magnet motors involves taking into account conflicting requirements from the point of view of electromagnetic and mechanical design. The authors focus on a particular technique to achieve high torque to magnet volume ratio while providing an adequate mechanical strength for the rotor. For this purpose the use of a can, which may consist of magnetic or nonmagnetic material, to contain the rotor is proposed. The authors present the results of computational and experimental investigations on the use of a solid steel can and its effect on the performance of motors having high energy magnets. Accurate modelling of a particular design, obtained using the 2-D finite element software package MOTOR-CAD, is also given. The results obtained by computation show good agreement with those obtained experimentally.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of switched reluctance drives by the finite element time-stepping method
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In the analysis of the performance of a switched reluctance drive, a common approach is to predict the flux linkages with a phase as a function of angle and current, neglecting coupling between phases. It appears that all this information could be derived by the use of a finite element time-stepping procedure extended from the procedures already successfully used on synchronous generators, induction motors and inverter-fed synchronous motors. The authors outline the method and discuss modelling of the motor and power converter. They also show the results of applying the method to a trial large switched reluctance drive.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Input current shaping in brushless DC motor drives utilizing inverter current control
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: It is proposed that the PWM inverter of a conventional brushless DC motor drive be treated as a buck converter. In particular, if the DC link capacitor is simply eliminated then a basic buck configuration current shaper can be realized. In this configuration the inverter switches can be used to control the motor current as before but can also be used indirectly to shape the average input current wave shape. In effect the control strategy hinges on the fact that the power to the rectifier pulsates unidirectionally at twice line frequency if the input current is sinusoidal and the power factor is unity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Post-assembly impulse magnetization of brushless DC motors equipped with rare-earth magnets
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The magnetization of fully dense and bonded forms of rare-earth magnets poses considerable problems due to their high magnetizing field requirements. The authors present a general methodology for the design of post-assembly magnetizing fixtures, albeit applied to radial-field topologies of brushless DC motor. The design details are established in three stages, the first of which estimates the peak MMF requirement, the second deduces the optimal disposition and number of conductors, and the third involves a detailed simulation of the complete impulse magnetization process. This latter step is based on the simultaneous time-stepped solution of the nonlinear differential equation governing the capacitor discharge magnetizer/fixture circuit and the transient diffusion equation governing the electromagnetic field with due account of heating of the fixture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Thermal analysis in an induction machine using thermal network and finite element methods
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Winding damage, except when caused by accidents, depends on the wear level of the windings themselves; the wear is a function of the time and of the temperature. This is why is is necessary, at the design stage, to foresee with a certain degree of accuracy the thermal stresses to which the electrical machine is subjected under rated operating conditions. The results obtained by the thermal network method (TNM) and by the finite element method, both used for the thermal field analysis of a three phase asynchronous motor with deep-bars and squirrel cage rotor, during steady-state operation, show that the calculated temperatures are within the limits required by standards. The use of FEM instead of TNM for calculating the temperature distribution is very important for the optimal design of the whole machine in general and of the rotor squirrel-cage in particular.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fully digital permanent magnet synchronous motor drive with flux weakening
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSM) are salient when designed with buried or interior magnets. Salient pole PMSM have shown better torque capability by utilising the reluctance torque, and may have a large flux weakening region when compared to the more common non-salient pole PMSM. A new approach for flux weakening in PMSM drives is presented, and a fast digital vector modulator with look-up tables is described. The control principles are verified by simulations and laboratory tests on a 2.8 kW salient pole PMSM drive.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparative study of slotted and slotless electronically-commutated permanent-magnet DC servomotors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Permanent-magnet excited DC servomotors with electronic commutation are becoming increasingly attractive in many applications due to their performance advantages such as reduced size and weight, high efficiency, low noise and maintenance, improved reliability and very good control characteristics in a wide speed range. The authors compare both slotted and slotless options for electronically-commutated neodymium-magnet DC servomotors on the basis of the torque capability for the same frame size and Joule's losses amount.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design and tests of a 6 MW, 10000 RPM induction motor
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The use of high speed electrical motors for direct driving of compressors may be very interesting in terms of installation or maintenance costs and reliability. During the 1980s; ACEC ENERGIE developed the concept of a high speed induction generator driven by two overhung impellers, using the expansion power of natural gas. The same concept of a central motor flanked by two overhung impellers has been used in an induction motor application, for natural gas pipeline compression stations. The authors describe this 6 MW, 10000 RPM application and also show how this high speed electrical motor design may comply with other industrial applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Finite-element simulation of a generator feeding into a rectified load
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A finite-element technique has been developed which permits the representation of electrical machines and their interaction with power electronic devices in much greater detail than was previously possible using circuit models. When finite-element and circuit models were compared for the simulation of transient behaviour (the start-up of a diode rectifier bridge and resistive load) the stator phase current and hence load current agreed well but with a sufficient degree of difference to suggest that the machine models used affect the commutation behaviour of the rectifier bridge differently. An unexpectedly short time period found in the finite-element simulation may be due to a data output error in the program.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An application of linear motor to loudspeaker systems
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors describe an application of linear motors to loudspeaker systems. The loudspeaker system being developed is based on a novel concept of woofer loudspeakers. It has the characteristics of linear drive, low distortion and nondirectional acoustic wave propagation. The basic electromagnetic parts of the new system are in the form of a low-inertia linear motor with a cylindrical configuration; the vibrating part is a piston which is made up of composite materials inlaid with a Nd-Fe-B permanent magnet acting as the moving secondary of the motor. The equivalent circuit of the whole system is developed based on the principle of electromechanical-acoustic analogy. A simulation model of the speaker system has been developed for analysis purposes. Some design criteria of the system are also discussed by the authors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Brushless DC motor with airgap windings-influence of back iron material on motor efficiency
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In applications using batteries as a power source, the focus is on high efficiency for the electromechanical energy converters. A disc-type motor is developed using permanent magnets for the rotor and an airgap winding for the stator. According to the type of control, this device will operate as a synchronous motor or a brushless DC motor. The backiron design also contributes to the envisaged low losses. The field and the losses are analytically calculated and compared with experimental values.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An examination of the scaling properties of electric micromotors and their magnetic duals
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Advances in silicon micromachining technology are such that small electric motors fabricated using integrated circuit technology may be able to compete with conventional magnetic motors in the future. While it is apparent that at extremely small scales electric actuation is favourable, it is not clear at what point this transition takes place. An examination of this question for one particular motor design is presented. The output coefficient of a twelve stator pole, eight rotor pole variable capacitance synchronous motor is determined and the dimensions of an equivalent magnetic machine are estimated. The influence of permanent magnets in the rotor structure of the magnetic machine is also considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Force ventilated motors-advantages in fixed and variable-speed applications
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The traditional design of industrial induction motors uses a radial fan mounted directly on the motor shaft to ensure adequate cooling during operation. This provides the lowest cost, most compact design and simplest construction for most fixed speed applications, where the induction motor dominates all other forms of drive technology. However, there is a growing need with variable speed applications for motors with improved cooling when operating at low speeds. The simplest way to achieve this is to provide a second, small, constant speed induction motor to drive the cooling fan. The use of force ventilated, or separately blown motors is not new, but the advent of static frequency inverters brings new life to the concept. The force ventilated motor offers several advantages when applied in a variable speed drive. The authors highlight these advantages for the benefit of prospective users. There are also some fixed speed applications where the force ventilated motor has an advantage which are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Losses and cooling of a high-speed and high-output power homopolar inductor alternator
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In order to support development of a high-speed and high-output power homopolar inductor alternator (1000-1500 kW, 16000 RPM), substantial research and engineering analyses were made. Attention is paid to the electromagnetic and heat transfer phenomena. Analysis is oriented to the specific components of the total losses, namely to the stray-load losses, caused by eddy currents in the rotor surface, and to the aerodynamic friction losses, caused by air turbulence in the airgap and in the end winding spaces. The origin, main decisive factors and conditions for generation of losses in question are thoroughly investigated. It is shown that these two losses component determine temperature of the rotor and of the stator winding. Therefore they also determine the maximum output power of a homopolar inductor alternator.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Heat distribution and thermal calculations for switched reluctance motors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The heat distribution in a prototype multi-tooth per stator pole switched reluctance motor, called the two-tooth or 12/10, is predicted. Calculations are carried out in two-dimensions (xy plane) and only the airgap conduction is assumed in the third dimension (z-axis). Conduction between the shaft of the motor and the body of machine is also taken into account. Calculations are done for the both natural and forced cooling and the calculated results are then compared with the experimentally obtained values for the forced cooling.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design and construction of medium power axial flux induction motors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A new approach for the design and construction of axial flux induction motors is presented. The design and construction procedure proposed was tested in the construction of a 25 HP and 240 RPM axial flux induction motor with an anisotropic rotor. Finally, a comparison between the rated characteristics of the axial flux motor with a traditional one is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Calculation of stall bar temperature rise
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A method has been described for the calculation of the stall temperature rise rate for the hottest bar in a rotor cage. It has also been demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally that this rise rate can differ very significantly from bar to bar in a machine of conventional design. The method for calculating the maximum bar temperature variation requires three basic steps. First the maximum bar current must be determined, and it has been shown that this can be accomplished via the conventional equivalent circuit. Secondly the loss distribution must be calculated, and this may be achieved using a simple stratified model of the bar and an impedance matrix. Finally a thermal model has been described, leading to a time-stepped finite difference solution for the bar temperature.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design criteria for brushless DC motors with hollow rotor of samarium cobalt for applications above 25000 RPM in vacuum
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Brushless permanent magnet DC motors have inherent low loss and low input as energy is also provided by the permanent magnet. The design criteria are discussed with the respect to the selection of magnetic materials, large airgaps, bearings, etc., highlighting reduction of mechanical stresses, noise and thermal barriers. The importance of electromagnetic design in relation to electronic controller and Hall sensor commutation are also discussed. Construction, design data and performance for two 2-pole motors are given. It is shown that a large radial airgap over 0.5 mm, which is not at all desirable in induction motors of similar sizes, can be easily achieved with samarium cobalt (SmCo) and neodymium iron boron (NdFeB) magnets.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The selection of an efficient electrical machine
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The user must select the appropriate machine for his requirements and then decide whether improvements in efficiency can be justified in terms of cost effectiveness. Incurring possible additional costs by ensuring an off-loaded start may allow the motor manufacturer to offer a more efficient machine. A complete analysis of the system as a whole including other operating costs is advisable before considering the benefits of improved motor efficiency in isolation. An ability to calculate all losses including stray with improved accuracy is essential to the motor manufacturer if he wants to offer the most suitable machine for the application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic taxonomy and modal analysis for vibration diagnosis
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors give a case study concentrating on the task of providing automatic aids to both diagnosis and prognosis by recognition of machine condition in the routinely monitored vibration signatures of turbine generator rotors. The target population of rotors is the two-pole, 660 MW turbine generator rotors designed and manufactured by the GEC Alsthom group. The signatures provided by GEC Alsthom are multi-sensor run-up and run-down signatures taken using tachometer pulse and tracking filter techniques. They consist of a number of phasor trajectories, amplitude and phase of transverse displacement at about 300 speed steps. The authors describe the automatic modal analysis of the signatures using the Kennedy-Pancu method and then discuss cluster-based reasoning. The problems encountered with real signatures and the results of simulated signatures are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A software approach to the measurement of terminal quantities for digital excitation control of turbine generators
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The excitation control system of a turbine generator is primarily required to control and protect the generator. The heart of the excitation control system is the automatic voltage regulator (AVR). The authors briefly describe the selection, software implementation and evaluation of techniques used for the measurement of terminal quantities in the digital AVR. A brief review of the popular measurement techniques in three-phase systems is presented. Practical considerations like sampling rate, processing power, accuracy, effect of harmonics, etc., are taken into account during the design of the software.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Switched reluctance drives for applications in hazardous areas
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Hazardous areas are normally defined as those places where a potentially flammable atmosphere exists. Electrical equipment for use in these areas must therefore have particular design and constructional features which enable them to operate safely. A large number of specifications and standards have been drawn up, both by users and national approvals agencies, to regulate the designs. Inevitably, these act as constraints on the designer, making his task more difficult. The authors consider the design of variable-speed drives which meet these constraints and give an illustration of a successful recent development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Current controller in synchronous reference frame for high performance AC drives
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Current controlled high performance AC drives (for spindles application for example) require quick current response in transient state and low harmonic current content in steady state. The authors propose a new current regulator in synchronous reference frame based on the space vector PWM. The voltage reference is obtained through the regulation of the fundamental harmonic of the torque and flux current components in synchronous reference frame, up to when the machine back EMF can be overcome. Complete simulation results are carried out in order to evaluate the validity of the proposed method in the whole speed range of operation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Topologies for a permanent magnet generator/speed sensor for the ABS on railway freight vehicles
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Antilock braking systems (ABS) are being considered for high-speed railway eight vehicles, which since they have no on-board electrical supply, require axle-mounted permanent magnet generators to provide a speed sensing control signal as well as the power for the solenoid valves which control the pneumatic brakes. The authors describe a design study on alternative topologies for such 3-phase generators, and present test results from prototype machines. They then go on to consider the implications of the choice of magnet material and pole number on the design of 'interior magnet' and 'surface-mounted magnet' machine topologies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Magnetic flux distribution in the end regions of high precision slab resolvers and synchros
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Small angle measurement devices such as resolvers and synchros depend, to a large extent, upon the close control of their magnetic field distribution for their high performance. The authors investigate the flux distribution in the end regions of such devices and consider methods of improving resolver and synchro design using numerical methods and computer modelling. An algorithm specifically developed for resolver and synchro analysis is used to show that a large flux density exists in the end regions, caused by the axial fringing and leakage flux becoming trapped in the end laminations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Output deviations in digitally controlled asynchronous motors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors deal with some problems raised by the application of digital control to asynchronous motors. At first the mathematical model of a digitally controlled asynchronous motor is described, which allows a step by step evaluation of the main electrical and mechanical motor quantities. Then, it is used to evaluate currents and torqued ripples due to the digitalization of signals processing and numerical examples are shown for a sample asynchronous motor and for different feeding algorithms. It is finally shown that an easy analytical law exits between torque deviations and sampling period and that it can successfully be used for control designing purposes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Stabilization and speed control of a hypersynchronous doubly-fed motor: tests and experimental results
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: An experimental research work is carried out in order to overcome the inherently unstable behaviour of doubly-fed hypersynchronous motors. The authors deal with the developed method which uses a frequency converter supply of either the rotor or stator winding of the machine, while the other machine winding is connected to the grid. The authors discuss the required control algorithm, and present the results of experimental tests carried out on a 6 hp machine. These results show that stable motor running conditions can be achieved, and converter operations allow a suitable control of the rotor speed over the synchronous speed set by the grid frequency.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation of a brushless DC motor control scheme with sliding mode control
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A control scheme for a prototype brushless DC motor is developed and a simulation study of the motor, inverter and controller is carried out to allow correct controller parameters to be selected. The simulation of the three phase system is carried out using TurboBASIC on a PC-compatible computer, and is extended to include simulation of the sliding mode controller.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A compact ultrasonic motor-actuated software system implementation using fuzzy reasoning-based controller
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The inherent performance of ultrasonic motor (USM) which is one of highlighted servo actuators includes the following favorable features; compactness in size and thickness, flexible design structure, lowered acoustic and magnetic noises in operation, and high-response due to low inertia. In addition to this, the USM can generate high-torque over an ultra low speed range as compared with the commonly-used electromagnetic motors of the same size. The authors consider the control strategy concerned with this USM from a practical point of view. They present the ultrasonic motor-actuated software servo system using fuzzy reasoning concepts. The fuzzy reasoning principle due to USM drive is introduced on the basis of the directly-driven positioning servo system applications. The experimental results of this system are illustrated and discussed practically.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Harmonic analysis of current waveforms in the DC link of a switched reluctance drive
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In applications where a switched reluctance (SR) drive is to be supplied from an AC network, its electronic power converter includes a rectifier, a DC link and a motor switching unit. The authors deal with the analysis of the harmonic content of current waveforms in the DC link for combinations of various rectifier topologies and SR motor switching unit topologies with associated controlling methods. The analysis has a qualitative character and it is used to shown the effect of these combinations on RMS capacitor current.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A 4 MW variable speed drive for a research and development aerodynamic wind tunnel
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The range of performance analyses and the technical challenges to be overcome when engineering a large drive system are described. To illustrate these points the design of a 4 MW wind tunnel impeller drive is used as a basis for discussion. This drive powers a 9 metre diameter aerodynamic wind tunnel fan at the Honda research and development centre in Tochigi, Japan and it is believed to be one of the largest drives used in this type of application. The use of an inverter fed synchronous motor in a wind tunnel is a rarity, DC drives having dominated this market for many years. However, the inverter fed AC drive offers distinct advantages over its DC counterpart, as is highlighted by the authors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Four-phase switched reluctance drive using pulse-width modulation control with four switches
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors describe the control strategy and operation of a power converter circuit for four-phase switched reluctance motor. The motor is based on an 8/6-salience magnetic configuration with associated star-connected windings power convertor topology. The control strategy is based on voltage-controlled pulse-width modulation applied to each phase, maximum overlap between conductions of adjacent phases and a priori control of switching angles. A four-phase switched-reluctance motor employing such control strategy is characterized with high efficiency over the operating range and with reduced torque ripple.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Large DC machines with the slotless armature
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A series of large DCV slotless machines manufactured by SKODA for rolling mill applications is special in that its design had to incorporate requirements for similar operating characteristics as these of classical DC machines. Particular attention was given to decreasing the additional losses in the active conductors of the armature while maintaining high magnetic flux and current densities, to minimize the excitation magnetomotive force and to suppressing the commutator bar voltage ripple by special design of the double parallel lap winding of the armature. Before the actual design started, the methods of solution including computer programs had to be elaborated for the calculation of magnetic fields.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Hybrid step motor with magnetic cores made of dielectromagnetic
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors carry out research to determine whether dielectromagnetics can be used for stators. A hybrid step motor is chosen for this study. Soft magnetic elements of the model motor (the rotor and the stator), are designed and made of dielectromagnetic material. The motor has a sheeted magnetic core stator and solid pole rotor. In addition, the design of the motor model incorporates the new technology of 'transfer sealing'.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Global vacuum and pressure impregnation of high voltage stator windings
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Global vacuum and pressure impregnation (v.p.i.) techniques for stator windings have been used on small output machines, i.e. below 2 or 3 MW for many years. It is now accepted practice to manufacture v.p.i. windings for machines up to 20-25 MW with line voltages to 13.8 kV. Units of this size, for general industrial drives, have been in service for at least 15 years and orders for larger machines and higher voltages are now being placed. The author describes the advantages of these large, high voltage, global vacuum and pressure impregnated windings. The author also describes two aspects of the system which differ from resin-rich windings and prompt most attention in end-users specifications, i.e., coil to core contact within the slot portion and the integrity of the end-winding bracing system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Asynchronous propulsion system for submarines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The author presents propulsion assemblies for submarines which include an asynchronous motor and a PWM frequency convertor. In order to provide dielectric strength and resist marine corrosion, motors are oil filled and pressure is equalised. The equipment is used for the propulsion of the submarine Nautile and its auxiliaries and the motor-drive of the on-board wire-guided robot ROBIN. The author describes methods considered and technical solutions selected taking account of special constraints for this deep water submarine capable of descending to 6000 meters and resisting pressure of 600 bars.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Large machines in hazardous atmospheres
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The author describes UK practices in the manufacture and use of large electric machines which are for applications other than for mining. The definition of 'large' is not precise, but here the emphasis is on machines of the so-called 'unit construction' type, which are those in which the stator, bearings and overall cover are mounted on a baseplate as separate units. The paper applies to both motors and generators and the precise form of construction is highly variable. The reliability and safety of such machines has been demonstrated by their service record but recently several incidents caused the UK industry to re-examine the manufacture and use of such machines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A microprocessor controlled induction motor by an adaptive indirect field orientation
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A 1.2 kW four-quadrant AC-drive is developed, in which the control is implemented with a microcomputer and the motor is supplied by a voltage-source inverter with current control using IGBTs. A self-adaptive scheme is described for automatically tracking the temperature and saturation dependent rotor time constant. The main advantage of this adaptive scheme is to merge two simple techniques without the use of additional sensors, while adding only a little more software overhead.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An ultra-pure water system for a hydro-electric generator-motor
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In 1979 the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board and GEC Large Machines Ltd. agreed to co-operate in the development of UK's first direct water-cooled hydro-electric generator-motor. The machine incorporates seven cooling water circuits, but only two require water of ultra-pure quality, i.e. having a conductivity of less than one micro Siemen per centimetre. These are the stator and rotor field winding circuits in which the cooling water is a direct connection between an electric potential and earth. Consequently the water has to be effectively nonconducting. The author describes the basic components of the system, the basic system concepts, hydraulic design, service experience and comparison with other systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A cycloconverter brushless cascaded induction motor
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The mathematical model of the brushless cascade machine supplied by impressed secondary stator current components is considered. The cascade speed range in which the primary stator is connected directly to a constant voltage, constant frequency supply and the secondary stator is supplied via a cycloconverter are shown to depend on the available cycloconverter frequency and machine torque development capability. For synchronous speed the electromagnetic torque is zero despite the presence of secondary stator current.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An unambiguous technique for displaying the presence of stator winding faults in induction motors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: It has been shown that the occurrence of shorted turns and phase imbalanced in the stator winding of induction motors cause predictable harmonics to appear in the spectrum of line currents and in the axial leakage flux. The authors show how such beating can itself be used as a measure of condition of the machine. The proposed technique extracts the changes in phase caused by the beat frequencies, and uses them to develop an alternative method of illustrating spectral changes. A simple computer based monitor has been developed using this technique, and results obtained using it are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On-line calculation of synchronizing and damping torque coefficients of a synchronous generator
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A method to calculate the synchronizing and damping torque coefficients was implemented on a personal computer and the experimental investigation was conducted on a laboratory system to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Results show that the performances of the proposed method are reasonably good. It is confirmed that the method can be used for monitoring the power system dynamic and steady-state stabilities on-line, only by using the data easily obtained from the generator and without knowing any information about the whole system. The calculated data could help the system planner to predict the stability for a future system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A flexible wave rotor reluctance machines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Flexible wave rotor reluctance machines are electromagnetic devices which serve to produce low rotational speed with high torque. These motors can be used in robot systems, space rockets, and special applications. They have an important advantage, since loads can be driven with very low speed (about 10 rev./min. or lower) without the need of a gearbox. In the present investigation, a new design for these wave machines employing a thin flexible rotor is proposed. The new design is characterized such that a high starting torque can be obtained. Also, a theoretical analysis used to calculate the contact force acts between the stator and the flexible rotor is given. A group of experimental results are used to demonstrate the performance characteristics and special feature of this machine.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Compulsators: principles and applications
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors discuss work being done on reducing and tailoring generator internal impedances in order to maximise their transient response. The work is taking place at the centre for Electromechanics at The University of Texas at Austin (CEM-UT). The resulting pulsed generators draw on the energy stored kinetically in the rotor inertia to generate extremely high power levels for short periods of time. Two classes of pulsed generators have been developed at CEM-UT: homopolar generators (single pulse) and compensated pulsed alternators or compulsators (repetitively pulsed). The authors discuss the developments of these two types of pulsed generators at CEM-UT and their principles and applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Surface motor drive control
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Until recently, indirect drive methods that convert rotary motion (such as from rotary motors and gears) into linear motion have been the main methods used for linear motion systems. Recently, however, advances in office and factory automation equipment have led to the development and commercialization of direct drive systems using linear surface (SFM) motors. In this paper, the authors describe the SFM's basic structure and operating principles, show the mathematical development that supports its bidirectional control system, and report on the results of prototype drive tests.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of high power linear pulse motor for artificial heart
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The authors deal with the results of the development of a linear pulse motor-driven artificial heart with left and right blood pumps. A small size and high thrust linear actuator is required in the development of such artificial hearts. In the present paper, the authors describe the structure and characteristics of these high power linear pulse motors. The results of a mock circulatory test of an artificial heart having two blood pumps which are driven by high power linear pulse motors are also described by the authors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sound intensity measurement on electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The sound power is the most important characteristic used for describing the noise emission from a machine. Its value is usually determined from sound pressure or sound intensity. The author presents results of sound intensity measurement on different types of electrical machine. The problems of the most suitable presentation of these results are discussed, not only for numerical ways but especially for graphical presentation. The variety depends on the possibilities of the software package used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of spreadsheet techniques as an aid to electrical machine/drive selection
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: A motor/drive selection problem is given as an example of the use of spreadsheet techniques. A selection process is particularly well suited to the 'what-if' aspect of spreadsheet usage. The solution proposed is not technically complex, but the routines developed require minimal development effort and eliminate the need for tedious repetitive manual calculations. They are envisaged as a way of relatively a designer of routine work. When fully automated, they should be readily usable by appropriate nondesign personnel with only a small period of initial familiarisation. The particular example chosen is the specification of a permanent-magnet DC servo motor required to meet a defined torque-speed load requirement.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On-line partial discharge detection in turbine generators
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The basic principles, design, and construction of a wide bandwidth directional coupler applied to on-line PD detection in operating turbine generators have been described. This device is known as the SSC. These couplers have been installed on a number of turbine generators. In each case PD has been successfully detected, in some cases in the presence of severe electrical noise. The basic premise under which the SSCs produce outputs and from which discrimination of PD from noise is possible, i.e. pulse shape, has been validated. This result implies that, in principle, the construction of an instrument which would have the ability to acquire the PD data while eliminating electrical noise is feasible. Currently, construction of such a device, known as the turbine generator analyzer (TGA), is underway.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling and control of fast, nonlinear electromechanical actuators for impact printing
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The author presents an illustration of the operational background of an impact matrix printhead. Then a realistic model for a typical clapper-type actuator is described. Furthermore, a new control scheme for improving the dynamic behaviour of the actuator in impact printing is discussed and some theoretical studies show the validity of the approach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Stator core end heating in air and hydrogen indirectly cooled turbogenerators
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Indirectly air-cooled machine and directly cooled machine end-region fields, losses and temperatures have been compared in detail. The losses in indirectly cooled machines are very substantially reduced due to a number of factors, the most dominant of which is the smaller air-gap length and lower electric loading. Other typical features, such as lower magnetic loadings and increased stator slot number also contribute to this reduction. For the two machines considered the eddy current losses in the stator core end on load are only 10% of that in the directly cooled machine. Three dimensional temperature calculations indicate that despite a poorer cooling circuit in an air-cooled machine the reduction in end-region losses is so great that only very moderate core end temperature rises occur as a result. The stator conductor bar operates at a considerably higher temperature than the core even in the end-region, and it is this feature which imposes the design limit. End-region losses are small enough to require only minimal additional design features in order to reduce them. The electric loading of air-cooled machines can be substantially increased before end-region losses become a major problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Operation of highly rated permanent magnet synchronous machines
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Many applications call for drives with very high power/torque per unit weight/volume. Typical examples are drives for aerospace actuation systems and for electric or hybrid automotive transmissions. Permanent magnet machines of various types are strong contenders for these applications and to get the most from a given frame size they will be designed with high electric and magnetic loadings. Drive specifications quite often call for constant torque over a limited low speed range followed by constant power over an extended high speed range. Usually the high speed range involves operation of the machine at the supply voltage ceiling with flux weakening. The problem is examined from the viewpoint of trying to establish operating conditions using fixed parameters based on unsaturated or saturated conditions in comparison to a full account of saturation. This study can be seen as being related to strategies that might be implemented in a controller for the drive of the chosen machine.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transient model of a permanent magnet synchronous motor integrated drive system
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: In the design of integrated drives, consisting of motor, power converter and controller, it can be advantageous to model the transient performance prior to fully implementing the hardware. This enables motor design parameters and control strategies to be evaluated prior to implementation. One possible approach to this would be to accurately synthesise the converter waveforms in the model . When considering pulse width modulated (PWM) inverter fed machines this task becomes complex due to the nature of the waveforms being used as the switching pattern is dependant on both voltage and frequency. A simplified approach is used where the waveforms are taken to be sinusoidal at all times, balanced load conditions are also assumed. This can be justified in PWM fed machines as the waveforms produced are close to sinusoidal. Also the harmonics that are produced tend to be of high order contributing to rotor losses but not significantly to torque production.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condition monitoring of induction motors
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Over the years the manfacturers of induction motors have tried their best to produce reliable induction machines for the motor industry. A good monitoring system which could detect rotor cage faults which may arise during manufacturing or ealy signs of impending motor failure in the rotor would therefore serve a very useful purpose. The author describes a very simple method of detecting a slight rotor asymmetry which generally signifies the beginning of rotor failures which, if left unattended, could lead to a much more serious stator damage or machine breakdownn.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A balanced calorimeter for measurement of induction motor losses
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: Improved means of accurately measuring induction motor losses are becoming increasingly important because of the ever-present pressure for higher efficiency and the difficulties in applying the accepted methods to motors supplied by power electronic drives. The balance calorimeter described by the authors overcomes the worst difficulties of traditional calorimetry, and provides a more direct, sensitive and accurate measurement of induction motor losses than either the segregation of losses or the input-output method; the cost of the equipment required is also less than for the other methods described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Characteristics of transportation-switch using X-Y linear induction motor (X-YLIM)
publicationTitle: 1991 Fifth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives (Conf. Publ. No. 341)
abstract: The conventional linear induction motor (LIM) transportation system consists mainly of one-dimensional reciprocating motions. Therefore, if switching is required, two methods are conceivable. One is to stop the vehicle temporarity and rotate it in the switching direction by driving a turntable, and the other is to horizontally shift the flexible transportation line to the object switch line. An experimental facility constructed for test purposes consists of a speed measuing device and two lines, one for straight running and the other for switching the running track. The authors analyze the relationships between track width, switch track radius, switch angle and length of switch track. The theoretically calculated characteristics are compared with experimental ones.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
